edits.html:
Angelman Syndrome and Its Genetic Look-Alikes

Happy, laughing child with seizures, ataxia and no words · NBME · which parent's chromosome 15 copy is missing?

Source vignette Pt — 3 yo F with a seizure disorder on valproic acid and strabismus; height and weight at the 25th percentile, head circumference at the 3rd · Exam — happy and excitable, smiles and laughs often; flat back of the head, prominent jaw, widely spaced teeth; repeated hand flapping; stiff-legged gait, needs help on stairs; short attention span; communicates with gestures and sounds, no words · Q — the most likely genetic defect; options spanned chromosome 15 deletions of maternal or paternal origin, a chromosome 7 deletion, an MECP2 mutation, trisomy 15 and trisomy 21
The decision point

A child with no words, seizures, microcephaly, a stiff-legged, ataxic gait and a happy, excitable manner with frequent laughter has Angelman syndrome. Hand flapping, a flat occiput, a prominent jaw, widely spaced teeth and strabismus support it. The usual cause is deletion of the maternally inherited 15q11-q13 region, which contains UBE3A (ubiquitin protein ligase E3A). In neurons, imprinting silences the paternal copy of UBE3A. Losing the maternal copy therefore leaves those neurons with no working gene.

The same region deleted from the paternal chromosome causes Prader-Willi syndrome. Prader-Willi follows loss of the paternally expressed genes of the region. It presents as a floppy newborn with a poor suck, followed by hyperphagia, obesity, hypogonadism and short stature.

A less common cause of Angelman syndrome is paternal uniparental disomy. Both chromosome 15s come from the father, so no maternal UBE3A copy is present even though nothing is deleted. Maternal uniparental disomy is the mirror cause of Prader-Willi syndrome.

Defining criteria Angelman syndrome — no active maternal copy of UBE3A in neurons, usually from a maternal 15q11-q13 deletion · Prader-Willi syndrome — no active paternal copy of the 15q11-q13 genes, usually from a paternal deletion · Imprinting — silencing of one parent's copy of a gene by DNA methylation · Uniparental disomy — both copies of a chromosome inherited from one parent
Developmental delay with a genetic syndrome: the differential
DiagnosisBrief illness scriptKey discriminatorWhy less likely here
Angelman syndrome: maternal 15q11-q13 deletion; paternal uniparental disomy less oftenSevere delay with little or no speech, seizures usually before age 3, microcephaly, ataxic gaitHappy, excitable manner with frequent laughter; hand flappingThe answer: every finding in this child fits
Prader-Willi syndrome: paternal 15q11-q13 deletion; maternal uniparental disomy in about a quarterFloppy newborn with a poor suck; hyperphagia and obesity in childhood; hypogonadism, short stature, cognitive impairmentHyperphagia and obesity after a hypotonic infancy; hypogonadismHer weight is at the 25th percentile, with no hyperphagia or hypogonadism
Rett syndrome: MECP2 (methyl-CpG binding protein 2) mutation, X-linked, mostly girlsNormal development for 6 to 18 months, then loss of speech and purposeful hand use; head growth slows; seizures, gait problems, scoliosisRegression after normal early development; hand wringingNo loss of skills is described, and her hands flap rather than wring
Williams syndrome: 7q11.23 deletion that includes the elastin geneOverfriendly, usually mild intellectual disability; broad forehead, periorbital fullness, wide mouth with full lips; hypercalcemia in infancyOverfriendliness with supravalvar aortic stenosisNo murmur, typical facies or hypercalcemia is described
Down syndrome: trisomy 21Hypotonia from birth, up-slanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, single palmar crease; heart defects and duodenal atresiaRecognizable at birth by the face, hands and low toneNone of its facial or hand features is described
Scenario bank
Pearls Other Angelman features include a fascination with water and a reduced need for sleep · DNA methylation analysis of 15q11-q13 is the first test. It detects deletion, uniparental disomy and imprinting defects · A normal methylation result does not exclude Angelman syndrome. A UBE3A (ubiquitin protein ligase E3A) mutation accounts for about 1 in 10 cases and needs gene sequencing
How NBME framed it The options named the genetic defect and parent of origin, not the syndrome; the two chromosome 15 deletions differed only by parent.
Pairs with Part I Aneuploidy: Reading the Newborn covers Down syndrome and the newborn picture of Prader-Willi syndrome. Ask: was the child floppy from birth, or delayed with seizures and laughter later? Part I Hypotonia in an Infant owns the methylation workup for Prader-Willi syndrome in a floppy infant. Part I Cerebral Palsy and the MRI Pattern carries Rett syndrome as a regression mimic. Ask: did the child lose skills, or never gain them?
Transferable rule When the options name a genetic defect, identify the syndrome from the phenotype first. For chromosome 15, laughter, seizures and ataxia mean the maternal copy is missing. Hyperphagia after a floppy infancy means the paternal copy is missing.
Unchecked attributeChromosome 15 deletion, paternally inherited — same region, other parent. This is Prader-Willi syndrome, with hypotonic infancy, then hyperphagia, obesity and hypogonadism.
Salient decoyMutation of MECP2 — Rett syndrome also affects girls with microcephaly, seizures and repetitive hand movements. It follows normal early development with regression, and the hands wring rather than flap.
Salient decoyChromosome 7 deletion — Williams syndrome also gives a sociable child, but with overfriendliness, elfin facies, supravalvar aortic stenosis and hypercalcemia.
True-fact-wrong-slotTrisomy 15 — a complete trisomy 15 is typically lethal before birth. Paternal uniparental disomy, with two paternal chromosome 15s, is the less common route to Angelman syndrome.
Class-vs-memberTrisomy 21 — Down syndrome is the most common chromosomal cause of intellectual disability. It shows at birth with hypotonia, up-slanting palpebral fissures and a single palmar crease, none of which is described.
